claim: Pressure injuries are extremely painful.
source: They are extremely painful (Girouard et al., 2008), costly to prevent and treat (Padula and Delarmente, 2019), and increase the risk of patient sepsis and death (Wassel et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Girouard et al., 2008

claim: Pressure injuries are costly to prevent and treat.
source: They are extremely painful (Girouard et al., 2008), costly to prevent and treat (Padula and Delarmente, 2019), and increase the risk of patient sepsis and death (Wassel et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Padula and Delarmente, 2019

claim: Pressure injuries increase the risk of patient sepsis and death.
source: They are extremely painful (Girouard et al., 2008), costly to prevent and treat (Padula and Delarmente, 2019), and increase the risk of patient sepsis and death (Wassel et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wassel et al., 2020

claim: Tissue death in pressure injuries can be caused by mechanical deformation, ischemia, or both.
source: Tissue death can be caused by mechanical deformation, ischemia, or both.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about pressure injury mechanisms

claim: Poor clearance of damage factors may have unappreciated importance in pressure injuries.
source: Ischemia is often studied as ischemia-reperfusion injury, but poor clearance of damage factors may have unappreciated importance (Gray et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gray et al., 2016

claim: Pressure injuries often heal poorly.
source: Pressure injuries often heal poorly (Mervis and Phillips, 2019), especially if they involve deeper layers such as muscle (Bouten et al., 2003; Preston et al., 2017), but the reasons are for poor quality and quantity of healing are not clear.
evidence: Supported by citations to Mervis and Phillips, 2019; Bouten et al., 2003; Preston et al., 2017

claim: Pressure injuries involving deeper layers such as muscle heal especially poorly.
source: Pressure injuries often heal poorly (Mervis and Phillips, 2019), especially if they involve deeper layers such as muscle (Bouten et al., 2003; Preston et al., 2017), but the reasons are for poor quality and quantity of healing are not clear.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bouten et al., 2003; Preston et al., 2017

claim: The reasons for poor quality and quantity of healing in pressure injuries are not clear.
source: Pressure injuries often heal poorly (Mervis and Phillips, 2019), especially if they involve deeper layers such as muscle (Bouten et al., 2003; Preston et al., 2017), but the reasons are for poor quality and quantity of healing are not clear.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap in the field

claim: Chronic ulcers of veins or arteries have high levels of extracellular hemoglobin released in the wound.
source: Chronic ulcers of veins or arteries (e.g., venous stasis ulcers, sickle cell ulcers) have high levels of extracellular hemoglobin (Hb) released in the wound.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about chronic ulcers

claim: Many chronic ulcers have deposits of hemosiderin.
source: For example, many have deposits of hemosiderin.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about chronic ulcers

claim: Extracellular hemoglobin and its breakdown products create oxidative stress.
source: Extracellular Hb and its breakdown products (e.g., hemin, iron) create oxidative stress (Goldman et al., 1998; Reeder and Wilson, 2005) and other effects that are detrimental to regeneration.
evidence: Supported by citations to Goldman et al., 1998; Reeder and Wilson, 2005

claim: Hemoglobin decreases nitric oxide for angiogenesis.
source: For example, Hb decreases nitric oxide for angiogenesis (Kato et al., 2017; Nader et al., 2020) and signals as a damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) to increase inflammation (Mendonça et al., 2016; Bozza and Jeney, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kato et al., 2017; Nader et al., 2020

claim: Hemoglobin signals as a damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) to increase inflammation.
source: For example, Hb decreases nitric oxide for angiogenesis (Kato et al., 2017; Nader et al., 2020) and signals as a damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) to increase inflammation (Mendonça et al., 2016; Bozza and Jeney, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mendonça et al., 2016; Bozza and Jeney, 2020

claim: Hemoglobin is an innate immune factor with evolutionarily conserved antimicrobial function.
source: Hb is also an innate immune factor with evolutionarily conserved antimicrobial function.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about hemoglobin function

claim: When extracellular hemoglobin is activated, it increases production of reactive oxygen species.
source: When extracellular Hb is activated by proteolytic cleavage, bacterial binding, or conformational change, it increases production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) Bogdan, 2007; this process has been called 'oxidative burst without phagocytes' (Bogdan, 2007; Jiang et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bogdan, 2007; Jiang et al., 2007

claim: Myoglobin release into plasma or urine has been observed after muscle pressure injuries in multiple studies.
source: Myoglobin release into plasma or urine has been observed after muscle pressure injuries (mPI) in multiple studies including deep tissue injury (DTI) (Traa et al., 2019; Makhsous et al., 2010; Loerakker et al., 2012; Levine, 1993; Traa, 2019), but was studied as a readout of damage rather than a source of damage.
evidence: Supported by citations to Traa et al., 2019; Makhsous et al., 2010; Loerakker et al., 2012; Levine, 1993; Traa, 2019

claim: An extracellular environment oxidizes globins to a ferric (Fe3+) state.
source: An extracellular environment oxidizes globins to a ferric (Fe3+) state, which can be further oxidized to ferryl (FeIV=O) globin in the presence of endogenous peroxides such as hydrogen peroxide (Reeder et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reeder et al., 2008

claim: Ferric globin can be further oxidized to ferryl globin in the presence of hydrogen peroxide.
source: An extracellular environment oxidizes globins to a ferric (Fe3+) state, which can be further oxidized to ferryl (FeIV=O) globin in the presence of endogenous peroxides such as hydrogen peroxide (Reeder et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reeder et al., 2008

claim: Hydrogen peroxide is ubiquitous in contexts of cell stress, mitochondrial permeabilization, and cell death.
source: Hydrogen peroxide is ubiquitous in contexts of cell stress, mitochondrial permeabilization, and cell death (Rojkind et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rojkind et al., 2002

claim: Ferryl-Mb can oxidize macromolecules directly.
source: Ferryl-Mb can oxidize macromolecules directly (Goldman et al., 1998; Kapralov et al., 2009; Plotnikov et al., 2009) and can form heme-to-protein crosslinks (Osawa and Williams, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Goldman et al., 1998; Kapralov et al., 2009; Plotnikov et al., 2009

claim: Ferryl myoglobin can form heme-to-protein crosslinks.
source: Ferryl-Mb can oxidize macromolecules directly (Goldman et al., 1998; Kapralov et al., 2009; Plotnikov et al., 2009) and can form heme-to-protein crosslinks (Osawa and Williams, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Osawa and Williams, 1996

claim: Ferryl myoglobin can participate in a catalytic cycle of pseudo-peroxidase activity (redox cycling).
source: Most importantly, ferryl myoglobin can participate in a catalytic cycle of pseudo-peroxidase activity (redox cycling) (Boutaud and Roberts, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boutaud and Roberts, 2011

claim: Myoglobin can induce ferroptosis in a tissue context.
source: In a tissue context, myoglobin can induce ferroptosis, which is a form of non-apoptotic cell death associated with iron and characterized by lipid peroxidation (Dixon et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dixon et al., 2012

claim: Deferoxamine (DFO) is an FDA-approved small-molecule iron chelator that improves iron overload syndromes.
source: Deferoxamine (DFO), also known as desferrioxamine or desferoxamine, is an FDA-approved small-molecule iron chelator that improves iron overload syndromes (Velasquez and Wray, 2022; Karnon et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Velasquez and Wray, 2022; Karnon et al., 2012

claim: DFO binds free iron and heme at a 1-to-1 ratio.
source: DFO binds free iron and heme at a 1-to-1 ratio (Velasquez and Wray, 2022), scavenges free radicals (Reeder et al., 2008; Morel et al., 1992), reduces ferryl myoglobin to ferric myoglobin (Plotnikov et al., 2009; Vanek and Kozhli, 2022), inhibits crosslinking of heme to protein (Reeder and Wilson, 2005), and prevents the formation of pro-oxidant globin and heme species.
evidence: Supported by citation to Velasquez and Wray, 2022

claim: DFO scavenges free radicals.
source: DFO binds free iron and heme at a 1-to-1 ratio (Velasquez and Wray, 2022), scavenges free radicals (Reeder et al., 2008; Morel et al., 1992), reduces ferryl myoglobin to ferric myoglobin (Plotnikov et al., 2009; Vanek and Kozhli, 2022), inhibits crosslinking of heme to protein (Reeder and Wilson, 2005), and prevents the formation of pro-oxidant globin and heme species.
evidence: Supported by citations to Reeder et al., 2008; Morel et al., 1992

claim: DFO reduces ferryl myoglobin to ferric myoglobin.
source: DFO binds free iron and heme at a 1-to-1 ratio (Velasquez and Wray, 2022), scavenges free radicals (Reeder et al., 2008; Morel et al., 1992), reduces ferryl myoglobin to ferric myoglobin (Plotnikov et al., 2009; Vanek and Kozhli, 2022), inhibits crosslinking of heme to protein (Reeder and Wilson, 2005), and prevents the formation of pro-oxidant globin and heme species.
evidence: Supported by citations to Plotnikov et al., 2009; Vanek and Kozhli, 2022

claim: DFO inhibits crosslinking of heme to protein.
source: DFO binds free iron and heme at a 1-to-1 ratio (Velasquez and Wray, 2022), scavenges free radicals (Reeder et al., 2008; Morel et al., 1992), reduces ferryl myoglobin to ferric myoglobin (Plotnikov et al., 2009; Vanek and Kozhli, 2022), inhibits crosslinking of heme to protein (Reeder and Wilson, 2005), and prevents the formation of pro-oxidant globin and heme species.
evidence: Supported by citation to Reeder and Wilson, 2005

claim: DFO can function as an activator of Hif1α.
source: DFO can function as an activator of Hif1α (Tchanque-Fossuo et al., 2017; Xiao et al., 2013), a tool for promoting angiogenesis (Duscher et al., 2015; Holden and Nair, 2019), an antioxidant (Sundin et al., 2000), or can join an anti-ischemic cocktail (Soloniuk et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tchanque-Fossuo et al., 2017; Xiao et al., 2013

claim: DFO can be used as a tool for promoting angiogenesis.
source: DFO can function as an activator of Hif1α (Tchanque-Fossuo et al., 2017; Xiao et al., 2013), a tool for promoting angiogenesis (Duscher et al., 2015; Holden and Nair, 2019), an antioxidant (Sundin et al., 2000), or can join an anti-ischemic cocktail (Soloniuk et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to Duscher et al., 2015; Holden and Nair, 2019

claim: DFO can function as an antioxidant.
source: DFO can function as an activator of Hif1α (Tchanque-Fossuo et al., 2017; Xiao et al., 2013), a tool for promoting angiogenesis (Duscher et al., 2015; Holden and Nair, 2019), an antioxidant (Sundin et al., 2000), or can join an anti-ischemic cocktail (Soloniuk et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sundin et al., 2000

claim: Pressure injuries are known to have gradual expansion of tissue death.
source: Pressure injuries are known to have gradual expansion of tissue death (Stadler et al., 2004), consistent with secondary progression, but blocking secondary progression has not been clinically recognized as a goal for intervention (European Pressure Ulcer Advisory Panel et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stadler et al., 2004

claim: Blocking secondary progression has not been clinically recognized as a goal for intervention in pressure injuries.
source: Pressure injuries are known to have gradual expansion of tissue death (Stadler et al., 2004), consistent with secondary progression, but blocking secondary progression has not been clinically recognized as a goal for intervention (European Pressure Ulcer Advisory Panel et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to European Pressure Ulcer Advisory Panel et al., 2019

claim: High levels of hemoglobin or heme/hemin can impair the survival, chemotaxis, and phagocytosis of phagocytic cells.
source: Our fourth and final additional hypothesis is inspired by prior studies of blood-related conditions in which high levels of hemoglobin or heme/hemin could impair the survival, chemotaxis, and phagocytosis (Nader et al., 2020; Ferris and Harding, 2019; Sindrilaru et al., 2011; Ballart et al., 1986; Liu et al., 2019; Martins et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2009; Yefimova et al., 2002) of phagocytic cells.
evidence: Supported by citations to Nader et al., 2020; Ferris and Harding, 2019; Sindrilaru et al., 2011; Ballart et al., 1986; Liu et al., 2019; Martins et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2009; Yefimova et al., 2002

claim: Despite comparable diameters of dead muscle between CTX and mPI at day 3, the wound diameters were vastly different at day 10.
source: Despite comparable diameters of dead muscle between CTX and mPI at day 3, the wound diameters were vastly different at day 10 (Supplementary file 1a; p=0.578 at day 3 and p<0.0001 at day 10).
evidence: Supported by data in Supplementary file 1a with statistical significance p=0.578 at day 3 and p<0.0001 at day 10

claim: In the CTX injury at day 3, many blood vessels were intact and carrying red blood cells.
source: In the CTX injury at day 3, many blood vessels were intact and carrying red blood cells, but in mPI at day 3, intact vasculature was not observed in the compressed region (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: In mPI at day 3, intact vasculature was not observed in the compressed region.
source: In the CTX injury at day 3, many blood vessels were intact and carrying red blood cells, but in mPI at day 3, intact vasculature was not observed in the compressed region (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: Pressure affects blood and lymphatic vessels in many ways including potentially loss of flow.
source: Prior work showed that pressure affects blood and lymphatic vessels in many ways including potentially loss of flow (Gray et al., 2016; Kimura et al., 2020; Karahan et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gray et al., 2016; Kimura et al., 2020; Karahan et al., 2018

claim: After CTX killed the panniculus muscle, substantial muscle regeneration occurred by 10 d, in which immature muscle fibers displayed central nuclei.
source: After CTX killed the panniculus muscle, substantial muscle regeneration occurred by 10 d, in which immature muscle fibers displayed central nuclei (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 1A

claim: At 40 d after acute CTX injury, muscle was completely regenerated and mature (evidenced by peripherally located nuclei).
source: At 40 d after acute injury, muscle was completely regenerated and mature (evidenced by peripherally located nuclei, Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 1C

claim: The pressure-injured wound bed remained filled with dead tissue at day 10.
source: In contrast, the pressure-injured wound bed remained filled with dead tissue at day 10 (Figure 1B and E–F; p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 1B and E–F with statistical significance p<0.0001

claim: Pressure injuries showed no signs of infection and no epibole.
source: Our pressure injuries showed no signs of infection and no epibole (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 1E

claim: The dead epidermis, dermis, dWAT, and panniculus layers were pushed upward at day 7 ± 2 as slough.
source: The dead epidermis, dermis, dWAT, and panniculus layers were pushed upward at day 7 ± 2 as slough (necroslough, per the nomenclature of Nasser, 2019) and remained at the surface, eventually becoming a dry eschar (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 1E

claim: When the eschar dropped off (by day 15), the size of the epithelial opening was smaller than the eschar, meaning that re-epithelialization had occurred underneath the eschar.
source: When the eschar dropped off (by day 15), the size of the epithelial opening was smaller than the eschar, meaning that re-epithelialization had occurred underneath the eschar.
evidence: Inference from observation of wound size changes

claim: Re-epithelialization completed at day 21 ± 2 in mPI.
source: Re-epithelialization completed at day 21 ± 2.
evidence: Observation from the study

claim: Despite successful closure of the epithelial layer, pressure injuries at 40 d had only partial regeneration of the panniculus carnosus layer.
source: Despite successful closure of the epithelial layer, pressure injuries at 40 d had only partial regeneration of the panniculus carnosus layer (Figure 1D and G; p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 1D and G with statistical significance p<0.0001

claim: At 90 d after pressure injury, the dermis and epidermis had regenerated, but a hole remained in the panniculus muscle layer.
source: At 90 d after pressure injury, the dermis and epidermis had regenerated, but a hole remained in the panniculus muscle layer (Figure 1H), indicating a failure to regenerate (Nasir et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 1H

claim: Both CTX-induced and pressure-induced injuries had comprehensive death of muscle tissue at day 3 post-injury.
source: Both CTX-induced and pressure-induced injuries had comprehensive death of muscle tissue, as indicated by karyolysis (dissolution of nuclear components), karyorrhexis (fragmentation of the nucleus), and acidification (eosinification) in H&E staining of the panniculus carnosus (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 2B

claim: Cells in pressure-injured tissues were flattened, and the thickness of the panniculus muscle layer was half of uninjured.
source: CTX and pressure injuries had a difference in morphology: cells in pressure-injured tissues were flattened, and the thickness of the panniculus muscle layer was half of uninjured (Figure 2A–C; p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 2A–C with statistical significance p<0.0001

claim: The muscle layer of CTX wounds had sixfold higher levels of immune cell infiltrate than mPI.
source: The muscle layer of CTX wounds had sixfold higher levels of immune cell infiltrate than mPI (p<0.0001; Figure 2A–B and D).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 2A–B and D with statistical significance p<0.0001

claim: The panniculus layer of mPI was nearly devoid of intact immune cells.
source: The panniculus layer of mPI was nearly devoid of intact immune cells.
evidence: Observation from the study

claim: Some viable immune cells were found at the margins of the mPI wound (at the boundary between injured and uninjured tissue), but not in the compressed region of mPI.
source: Some viable immune cells were found at the margins of the wound (at the boundary between injured and uninjured tissue), but not in the compressed region of mPI (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Iron-scavenging is performed by macrophages.
source: The absence of immune cell infiltrate is noteworthy because iron-scavenging is performed by macrophages (Kristiansen et al., 2001; Soares and Hamza, 2016), and because free iron, when not adequately scavenged, can overstimulate the innate immune response (Bessman et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kristiansen et al., 2001; Soares and Hamza, 2016

claim: Free iron, when not adequately scavenged, can overstimulate the innate immune response.
source: The absence of immune cell infiltrate is noteworthy because iron-scavenging is performed by macrophages (Kristiansen et al., 2001; Soares and Hamza, 2016), and because free iron, when not adequately scavenged, can overstimulate the innate immune response (Bessman et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bessman et al., 2020

claim: Levels of citH3 were tenfold higher in mPI than in CTX at day 3 wounds.
source: In day 3 wounds, levels of citH3 were tenfold higher in mPI than in CTX (Figure 2E–G; p=0.0280).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 2E–G with statistical significance p=0.0280

claim: Highest levels of citH3 occurred near the muscle layer, such as the interface between the panniculus layer and the dWAT or dermis.
source: Highest levels occurred near the muscle layer, such as the interface between the panniculus layer and the dWAT or dermis.
evidence: Observation from the study

claim: Oxidative stress is a well-studied trigger of ETosis.
source: This is consistent with the possibility that immune cells may have been present in the muscle layer of mPI before day 3 and then died of ETosis. Oxidative stress is a well-studied trigger of ETosis, and other stimuli include hemin and heme-activated platelets (Okubo et al., 2018; Ohbuchi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Okubo et al., 2018; Ohbuchi et al., 2017

claim: Hemin and heme-activated platelets are stimuli for ETosis.
source: This is consistent with the possibility that immune cells may have been present in the muscle layer of mPI before day 3 and then died of ETosis. Oxidative stress is a well-studied trigger of ETosis, and other stimuli include hemin and heme-activated platelets (Okubo et al., 2018; Ohbuchi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Okubo et al., 2018; Ohbuchi et al., 2017

claim: Iron deposition was very high in mPI, as measured by Perls' Prussian blue stain.
source: Iron deposition was very high in mPI, as measured by Perls' Prussian blue stain (Figure 2I), but iron was undetectable at the same time point after CTX injury (Figure 2H–J; p=0.0332).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 2I with statistical significance p=0.0332

claim: Iron was undetectable at day 3 after CTX injury.
source: Iron deposition was very high in mPI, as measured by Perls' Prussian blue stain (Figure 2I), but iron was undetectable at the same time point after CTX injury (Figure 2H–J; p=0.0332).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 2H–J with statistical significance p=0.0332

claim: Prussian blue detects accumulation of ferric Fe3+, typically in the form of ferritin and hemosiderin.
source: Prussian blue detects accumulation of ferric Fe3+, typically in the form of ferritin and hemosiderin, but it only shows high levels of iron, because it is unable 'to detect iron except in massive deposition' (Perl and Good, 1992; Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Perl and Good, 1992; Liu et al., 2014

claim: Levels of myoglobin were elevated in mPI compared to CTX injury.
source: Levels of myoglobin and hemoglobin were also elevated in mPI compared to CTX injury (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; p=0.0091 for myoglobin and p=0.0474 for hemoglobin).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 with statistical significance p=0.0091

claim: Levels of hemoglobin were elevated in mPI compared to CTX injury.
source: Levels of myoglobin and hemoglobin were also elevated in mPI compared to CTX injury (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; p=0.0091 for myoglobin and p=0.0474 for hemoglobin).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 with statistical significance p=0.0474

claim: HO-1 was expressed by mPI wound tissues at similar levels to CTX-injured tissue.
source: Heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) is an enzyme that performs heme degradation and serves as a marker of high heme or iron. HO-1 was expressed by mPI wound tissues, at similar levels to CTX-injured tissue (Figure 2K–M; p=0.998).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 2K–M with statistical significance p=0.998

claim: HO-1 expression was localized to the panniculus layer after CTX injury, but it was widespread across all layers after mPI.
source: However, HO-1 expression was localized to the panniculus layer after CTX injury, but it was widespread across all layers after mPI (Figure 2K–L).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 2K–L

claim: Prior studies of adult Mb−/− mice found no obvious phenotype.
source: Note that prior studies of adult Mb−/− mice found no obvious phenotype (Garry et al., 1998; Gödecke et al., 1999; Meeson et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Garry et al., 1998; Gödecke et al., 1999; Meeson et al., 2001

claim: Mb−/− is often lethal to cardiac development during E9.5-E10.5, but some Mb−/− embryos survive to term.
source: Mb−/− is often lethal to cardiac development during E9.5-E10.5, but some Mb−/− embryos survive to term (Meeson et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Meeson et al., 2001

claim: Among Mb−/− mice that were born, all developed with normal feeding, weight gain, grooming, social behavior, and life span.
source: Among our Mb−/− that were born, all developed with normal feeding, weight gain, grooming, social behavior, and life span.
evidence: Observation from the study

claim: Deletion of Mb was confirmed by western blotting, immunostaining, and DNA gel electrophoresis.
source: Deletion of Mb was confirmed by western blotting (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), immunostaining (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C), and DNA gel electrophoresis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by observations in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B, C, and D

claim: Mb−/− mice had increased capillary density (by 17%) compared to Mb+/+ mice.
source: With H&E staining, we detected no knockout-induced changes to the tissues of our injury model (skin, panniculus carnosus layer, or loose areolar tissue) other than increased capillary density (by 17%, p=0.0455; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) and increased thickness of the dWAT layer in Mb−/− mice (by 43%, p=0.0232, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E with statistical significance p=0.0455

claim: Mb−/− mice had increased thickness of the dWAT layer (by 43%) compared to Mb+/+ mice.
source: With H&E staining, we detected no knockout-induced changes to the tissues of our injury model (skin, panniculus carnosus layer, or loose areolar tissue) other than increased capillary density (by 17%, p=0.0455; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) and increased thickness of the dWAT layer in Mb−/− mice (by 43%, p=0.0232, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E with statistical significance p=0.0232

claim: Total iron was not significantly decreased in Mb−/− mice.
source: Total iron was not significantly decreased (p=0.0664, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F with p=0.0664

claim: At day 3 post-injury, Mb+/+ mice had high levels of iron in the muscle, dWAT, and dermis.
source: At day 3 post-injury, Mb+/+ mice had high levels of iron (Figure 3A), which appeared in the muscle, dWAT, and dermis, including both the extracellular space and in the small numbers of infiltrating immune cells.
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 3A

claim: Mb−/− mice had no detectable signal from Perls' stain in any layer of the wound at day 3 post-injury.
source: In contrast, Mb−/− mice had no detectable signal from Perls' stain in any layer of the wound (Figure 3B and C; p=0.0020).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 3B and C with statistical significance p=0.0020

claim: HO-1 was decreased by 57% in Mb−/− mPI compared to Mb+/+.
source: HO-1 was also decreased by 57% in Mb−/− mPI compared to Mb+/+ (Figure 3D–F; p=0.0438).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 3D–F with statistical significance p=0.0438

claim: Levels of immune cell infiltrate were 233% greater in Mb−/− compared to Mb+/+.
source: Levels of immune cell infiltrate were 233% greater in Mb−/− compared to Mb+/+ (Figure 3G–I; p=0.0250).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 3G–I with statistical significance p=0.0250

claim: The wound size was smaller in Mb−/− versus Mb+/+ at day 3.
source: The wound size was smaller in Mb−/− versus Mb+/+ (p=0.0297 at day 3, measured as external area, Figure 3J and Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 3J and Supplementary file 1c with statistical significance p=0.0297

claim: Histopathology scoring in the center of the wound showed 50% decreased tissue death in Mb−/− compared to Mb+/+.
source: Histopathology scoring in the center of the wound showed 50% decreased tissue death (p=0.0016, Figure 3G, H and K).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 3G, H and K with statistical significance p=0.0016

claim: DNA damage (8-OG) was decreased by 87% in Mb-knockout wounds.
source: Oxidative damage was lower in Mb-knockout wounds: DNA damage (8-hydroxy-2'-deoxyguanosine [8-OG]) was decreased by 87% (p=0.0485; Figure 4A–E), and lipid peroxidation (measured using BODIPY 581/591) was decreased by 61% (p=0.0298; Figure 4F–J).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 4A–E with statistical significance p=0.0485

claim: Lipid peroxidation was decreased by 61% in Mb-knockout wounds.
source: Oxidative damage was lower in Mb-knockout wounds: DNA damage (8-hydroxy-2'-deoxyguanosine [8-OG]) was decreased by 87% (p=0.0485; Figure 4A–E), and lipid peroxidation (measured using BODIPY 581/591) was decreased by 61% (p=0.0298; Figure 4F–J).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 4F–J with statistical significance p=0.0298

claim: Mb−/− had roughly 56% decrease in CitH3.
source: Similarly, Mb−/− had roughly 56% decrease in CitH3 (p=0.0127; Figure 4K–Q).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 4K–Q with statistical significance p=0.0127

claim: 3-nitrotyrosine showed a 56% decrease in Mb−/− wounds.
source: An additional measure of oxidative damage, 3-nitrotyrosine, showed the same pattern (56% decrease, p=0.0328; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 with statistical significance p=0.0328

claim: After pre-incubation with pro-inflammatory stimuli, RAW264.7 cells showed an increase in ROS in response to Mb treatment.
source: We also measured the impact of Mb on a monocyte/macrophage cell line in vitro. After pre-incubation with pro-inflammatory stimuli, RAW264.7 cells showed an increase in ROS and decrease in phagocytosis (measured as impaired efferocytosis or clearance of dead cells) in response to Mb treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by observation in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: After pre-incubation with pro-inflammatory stimuli, RAW264.7 cells showed a decrease in phagocytosis in response to Mb treatment.
source: We also measured the impact of Mb on a monocyte/macrophage cell line in vitro.
